content: Patients should strictly follow the recommended course of action, as adherence to these guidelines is a critical measure of high-quality healthcare. For policymakers, a strong recommendation implies that it can be widely adopted as a policy in most scenarios. The considerations used by the guideline advisory group to determine the strength of recommendations are detailed in Annex 2. Pregnant women, including adolescents and adults, should begin iron and folic acid supplementation as early as possible during pregnancy. In areas where anemia in pregnancy is a severe public health issue (affecting 40% or more of pregnant women), a daily dose of 60 mg of elemental iron is preferred over lower doses. Once a woman’s hemoglobin levels normalize, she can transition to the standard antenatal dose to prevent anemia recurrence. Folic acid requirements increase during pregnancy due to the rapid cell division in the fetus and increased urinary losses. Since the neural tube closes by day 28 of pregnancy, folic acid supplementation initiated after the first month will not prevent neural tube defects but will still benefit maternal and fetal health. Iron supplements should be provided even if folic acid is unavailable. In addition to iron and folic acid, supplements may include other vitamins and minerals, as per the United Nations Multiple Micronutrient Preparation guidelines, to address other potential maternal micronutrient deficiencies. Programs should also include measures such as hookworm control and referral systems for managing severe anemia cases. A behavior change communication strategy is essential to educate about the benefits of supplementation, manage side effects, and ensure the provision of high-quality supplements with appropriate packaging. This strategy can also promote dietary diversity and food combinations that enhance iron absorption. Oral supplements are available in various forms, such as capsules, soluble tablets, dissolvable tablets, and modified-release tablets. A robust quality assurance process is necessary to ensure that supplements are manufactured, packaged, and stored in a controlled and uncontaminated environment. Operational challenges related to improving the delivery and utilization of these interventions, as well as their effects on fetal growth and the programming of chronic diseases, require further research. Dissemination of the current guidelines will occur through electronic media, including slide presentations, CDs, the WHO nutrition website, and other platforms. The guidelines will also be shared with international partners, WHO offices, ministries of health, universities, and NGOs. They will be published in the WHO Reproductive Health Library and adapted to the context of each Member State. Before implementation, iron supplementation programs should have clear objectives that consider available resources, existing policies, delivery platforms, communication channels, and stakeholders. Ideally, iron and folic acid supplementation should be part of an integrated antenatal and neonatal care program. To improve implementation in lowand middle-income countries, the WHO Department of Nutrition for Health and Development collaborates with the Evidence-Informed Policy Network (EVIPNet), which fosters partnerships between policymakers, researchers, and civil society to facilitate evidence-based policy development. Monitoring and evaluation plans with appropriate indicators are encouraged at all stages of guideline implementation. The WHO Department of Nutrition for Health and Development is developing a centralized platform to share information on global nutrition actions, including programmatic details, country-specific adaptations, and lessons learned. The guideline development process followed WHO’s evidence-informed procedures, as outlined in the WHO handbook for guideline development. The WHO Steering Committee for Nutrition Guidelines Development, established in 2009, oversaw the process. Additional groups, including an advisory guideline group and an External Experts and Stakeholders Panel, were formed to provide input on the scope, questions, and outcomes of the guideline. The Nutrition Guidance Expert Advisory Group, established in 2009, includes subgroups on micronutrients, diet and health, nutrition across the life course, and monitoring and evaluation. This group advises WHO on decision-making outcomes and evidence interpretation. Efforts were made to include experts from diverse disciplines, regions, and stakeholder groups, excluding representatives from commercial organizations. The guideline questions were developed using the Population, Intervention, Control, Outcomes (PICO) format and reviewed by the Steering Committee and stakeholders. Evidence was summarized and appraised using the Cochrane methodology and the GRADE approach, which assesses study design, limitations, consistency, directness, and precision of evidence. The draft recommendations were reviewed and voted on by the guideline development group, considering the intervention’s effects, evidence quality, values, preferences, and costs. Conflicts of interest were managed according to WHO guidelines. All participants submitted declarations of interest and verbally disclosed potential conflicts at the start of each meeting. Feedback on the draft guideline was solicited through a public call, and the final guideline was submitted for WHO clearance before publication.
